parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State two advantages of the transmission of data in digital form, rather than analogue form.

markscheme_points.text: Any 2 from: $\bullet$ noise can be filtered out / noise can be removed; $\bullet$ can carry more information per unit; $\bullet$ can have extra bits of data to check; $\bullet$ can be encrypted

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to a signal as it travels - unwanted extra fluctuations get added. Why is it easier to clean up a signal that only has two distinct levels (0 and 1) than one that varies smoothly?
Hint 2: Think about what else you can do with 0s and 1s besides just sending the message - how could you add security, check for mistakes, or pack in more types of information at once?
parts.proper_answer: Any two from: noise can be filtered out / signal can be regenerated; can carry more information per unit time; extra parity bits can be added to check for errors; signal can be encrypted for security.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why digital is cleaner - noise**
Think of analogue as a smooth sloping hill and digital as steps that are either up or down. When noise adds a little wobble, the smooth hill is permanently distorted. With steps, you can still clearly tell if it was meant to be high or low, so you can rebuild the perfect original. This is called regeneration and filtering out noise.

Step 2: **Why digital is smarter - capacity, checking and security**
Because everything is numbers, you can do clever processing. You can multiplex to carry much more information, you can add extra check bits to detect and correct errors, and you can encrypt the 0s and 1s so only the intended receiver can decode them.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: Optic fibres are used for the transmission of data.
parts.text:
A signal in an optic fibre is carried by an electromagnetic wave of frequency $1.36 \times 10^{14} \text{Hz}$. The speed of the wave in the fibre is $2.07 \times 10^{8} \text{m s}^{-1}$.

For this electromagnetic wave, determine the ratio:
$$\frac{\text{wavelength in free space}}{\text{wavelength in fibre}}. $$
hints: Hint 1: When the same wave moves from free space into the fibre, one quantity stays exactly the same while speed and wavelength both change. Focus on how $v$ and $\lambda$ must change together.

Hint 2: Write each wavelength using speed divided by that common quantity, then see what cancels when you divide the two wavelengths. Remember to use $3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ for free space.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link wavelength to speed**
You have the same electromagnetic wave with frequency $f = 1.36 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ in two media. Frequency $f$ is set by the source and does not change. From $v = f\lambda$, we get $\lambda = v/f$. So at fixed $f$, wavelength is directly proportional to speed: $$\lambda \propto v$$

Step 2: **Turn wavelength ratio into speed ratio**
That means: $$\frac{\lambda_{free}}{\lambda_{fibre}} = \frac{v_{free}/f}{v_{fibre}/f} = \frac{v_{free}}{v_{fibre}}$$ In free space $v_{free} = c = 3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and in fibre $v_{fibre} = 2.07 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. So: $$\text{ratio} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^8}{2.07 \times 10^8} = 1.45$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The attenuation per unit length of the signal in the fibre is $0.40 \text{dB km}^{-1}$. The input power is $1.5 \text{mW}$ and the output power is $0.060 \text{mW}$.

Calculate the length of the fibre.
hints: Hint 1: Attenuation in dB compares input and output powers with a logarithm. Think about which power goes on top to give a positive loss when power drops along the fibre.
Hint 2: The total loss in dB is also built up steadily along the fibre. Think about how the given loss per km of $0.40 \text{ dB km}^{-1}$ links to total loss and length $L$.
Hint 3: Combine the two ideas for total loss to form one equation in $L$, then evaluate the log term with $1.5 \text{ mW}$ and $0.060 \text{ mW}$ and solve for $L$ in km.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Total attenuation from powers**
Attenuation measures how much the signal power has dropped, in decibels. For input power $P_{in}$ and output power $P_{out}$: $$\text{attenuation (dB)} = 10 \log\left(\frac{P_{in}}{P_{out}}\right)$$ Here $P_{in} = 1.5 \text{ mW}$ is larger than $P_{out} = 0.060 \text{ mW}$, so the ratio is greater than 1 and the log is positive, as expected for a loss.

Step 2: **Link total attenuation to length**
Loss builds up uniformly, so total loss equals loss per unit length times length: $$\text{attenuation} = (0.40 \text{ dB km}^{-1}) \times L$$ Equate the two expressions: $$0.40L = 10 \log\left(\frac{1.5}{0.060}\right)$$

Step 3: **Calculate L**
Evaluate the log: $$\frac{1.5}{0.060} = 25$$ $$10 \log(25) = 13.98 \text{ dB}$$ Then: $$L = \frac{13.98}{0.40} = 35 \text{ km}$$ The mW units cancel in the ratio, leaving $L$ in km to match the $\text{dB km}^{-1}$ unit.
